newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Lax controls raise doubts about Bosnia election.
newsitem.headline: Lax controls raise doubts about Bosnia election.

text.p: Lax supervision at polling stations and an improbably high voter turnout cast doubt on the integrity of Bosnia's first postwar elections, diplomats and independent monitors say.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, which oversaw the September 14 elections, had to recount a large portion of the vote after detecting major errors by locally- staffed counting houses.
The recount confirmed crushing victories by the very nationalist party factions that tore apart Bosnia in war.
OSCE election directors and an OSCE-affiliated observer team said the voting was widely free of the sort of fraud or other abuses that would warrant a decision not to certify it.
But independent monitors and some diplomats say the OSCE's figures do not add up according to the "one man-one vote" benchmark of clean, democratic elections.
"A comparison of figures suggests the turnout on September 14 was a mathematical impossibility," said the International Crisis Group, a think tank monitoring Bosnmia's peace process.
"We have no evidence to suggest (major) fraud but the discrepancies cast serious doubt on the validity of the elections," the ICG said in a report issued on Monday.
Going into the elections, the OSCE estimated the total electorate at 2.92 million. It announced on Election Day that "60-70" percent had voted, a "moderate turnout".
ICG calculations showed that about 259,000 war refugees did not register to vote. Another 381,000 who did register ended up not voting. This cut the maximum voter pool to 2,341,100.

According to preliminary final results released on Monday after a recount to weed out duplications, 2,616,935 ballots were cast for a new Bosnian collective presidency and 2,395,952 valid ballots for a House of Representatives.
These figures point to implausible voter turnouts of 111 percent for the presidency and 103 percent for the House.
A stunned OSCE summarily revised its estimate of the total electorate to about 3.2 million, but without producing any concrete documentation or rationale.
Even with the raised estimate, turnout would still have been over 90 percent -- a threshold historically equalled only in the rigged one-party elections of old Communist countries.
Turnout in Bosnia's 1990 presidency elections was 74 percent -- before scores of thousands of people died or went missing and 2.5 million were displaced in a 43-month-long war.
Independent observers witnessed only three cases of ballot box stuffing among 4,400 polling stations.

"But our demographic statistician monitoring the vote has concluded that 200,000 votes at minimum were produced by ballot-box stuffing or by local election committees (LECs), who were installed by nationalist state parties, cooking the count," an informed Western official told Reuters.

He said about 70 percent of the polling stations were left unsupervised by the OSCE "at the moment of closing". Many of these stations were in remote locations deliberately chosen by nationalist parties to minimise visits by refugee voters.
"There was nothing to prevent the LECs from picking up piles of unused ballots, ticking off their own parties and dropping them in the boxes," he said.
The OSCE deployed only one supervisor for every three polling stations and only one observer for every five.
The dominant Moslem, Serb and Croat nationalist parties which romped to electoral victory in their respective enclaves have curiously made no issue of impossible turnouts.

Ballot-box stuffing would have damaged mainly the ruling nationalists' nascent internal opposition, who seek to reunify Bosnia's communities. Rival party election observers were refused access to most polling stations.
After certification, expected this weekend, international peace coordinators will have the uphill task of pushing Moslem, Serb and Croat leaders into forming a new union government.
"These elections should not be certified," the ICG said. "If they are, the international community will have seriously undermined its credibility."

Diplomats say certification is pre-ordained by pressure from the U.S. government, author of the peace process, which wants to set the stage for a pullout of U.S. peace troops from Bosnia before American elections on November 5.
